paragraphs.point: Damage travels along a chain and is governed by the water state, not the rainfall anomaly alone
Monitoring is most complete for the deficit and least for the impact state
A forecast of the deficit is not a forecast of the damage
Impact depends on when and where the deficit lands, and is thresholded region by region
Onset speed is a second dimension, and what flash drought means is unsettled
The open question is anticipation: linking forecastable water states to impact thresholds

nodes.text: Impact is governed by the water state soil and vegetation experience, not the rainfall anomaly alone
Monitoring has been organized around the deficit
Global systems assemble near-real-time indicators into maps; some add seasonal probabilistic prediction
In-situ indices measure a point and cannot show regional development
Satellite records are limited by length and by spatial, temporal and spectral resolution
Monitoring is most complete where the deficit is measured and least where the impact is decided
Forecasting has taken a parallel path
Methods broadened from statistical, dynamical and hybrid systems to machine and deep learning
Soil-moisture predictability now extends from seasonal to decadal horizons
Limit 1: human water use weakens the hydrological-meteorological link (Yellow River basin)
Limit 2: impact forecasts depend greatly on the availability of impact records
A forecast of the deficit is not a forecast of the damage
nodes.evidence: 待补 (related: 12 C7, C8 on hazard-forecast skill)

nodes.text: Damage depends on when and where the deficit lands, not only on its size
Yield loss is tied to the growth stages at which evaporative stress peaks
nodes.evidence: 13 brazil-2016-evaporative-stress C1 (partial: ESI-yield correlation peaks at sensitive growth stages)

nodes.text: Leaf-area sensitivity to soil moisture has increased across many semi-arid and arid regions
The deficit at which vegetation responds varies from region to region
In European forests the water availability-mortality relationship is threshold-like
Global aggregates conceal this: no general forest drying trend, large spatial variability
Impact has no single global trajectory; thresholds must be located region by region
Onset speed adds a second dimension to the same problem
Flash-drought research has grown rapidly in two decades
Agreement on the term is incomplete: rate of intensification versus duration
Frequency, predictability and trend estimates inherit that choice
Whether flash drought is the 'new normal' is unresolved, since slow droughts may be increasing too
What remains unresolved is anticipation, not detection
Water states that forecasts can deliver

The present literature does not yet make that connection; it is this article's question
